title: Love Tough
author: Adrian Neibauer
summary: After finishing fall parent conferences, fifth-grade teacher Adrian Neibauer reflects on whether a pedagogy of care is enough. Parents praised how happy their children are in his class, which affirms his belief that students learn best when they feel safe and that belonging comes before curriculum. But in a new school with a young, chatty class where over half struggle to read at grade level, he worries that he has been caring more than teaching. He draws on his own experience as a father of two dyslexic children, whom he pushed hard, and on a childhood with one authoritarian and one laissez-faire parent, to think about balancing warmth and high expectations. He admits that a typical overcrowded classroom cannot deliver the daily small-group reading instruction he would like and that the direct instruction versus inquiry debate feels futile when behavior consumes the day. The post closes with resources on care, dyslexia and conferencing.
points: A pedagogy of care builds happiness and belonging, but love alone cannot teach students to read and write.
Large classes with many students below grade level make small-group instruction nearly impossible and exhaust the teacher.
Personal history as a child and as a father of dyslexic children shapes how the author balances support and high expectations.
Strong relationships and psychological safety are necessary conditions for learning, but they need sound instruction alongside them.
quotes: What credibility I lacked, I now have in abundance. I have been teaching a long time and know what I am doing.

Experience has taught me that unhappy students (or unhealthy, stressed, overwhelmed) struggle to learn; not because they cannot learn, but because they are struggling in ways that make it difficult for them to access their learning.
When students feel a strong sense of belonging and psychological safety, they are more likely to learn at high levels.
But with so many of my students partially progressing toward grade level, I ended the week reflecting on whether my care for my students is enough.
I realize that unfeigned love cannot solely teach students how to read and write.

In a perfect system, I would meet with small groups of students every day to practice whichever reading skills they need (fluency, phonological and phonemic awareness, vocabulary, comprehension, etc.). While I am meeting with groups of three-four students, the rest of the class would quietly work independently.
Direct instruction versus inquiry-based learning is a futile discussion when students are fighting, rolling around on the floor, or unable to pay attention for longer than five seconds.
As a parent, we try to give our children what we did not receive from our own parents, and so I love my children fiercely.
